results.content: Basically, for something to be truly reproducible, it has to respect the following bullet points: • Source code must obviously be available and thoroughly tested and documented (which is why we will be using Git and Github); 1https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/9187 17 1 Introduction • All the dependencies must be easy to find and install (we are going to deal with this using dependency management tools); • To be written with an open source programming language (nocode tools like Excel are by default non-reproducible because they can’t be used non-interactively, and which is why we are going to use the Python programming lan-guage); • The project needs to be run on an open source operating system (thankfully, we can deal with this without having to install and learn to use a new operating system, thanks to Docker); • Data and the paper/report need obviously to be accessible as well, if not publicly as is the case for research, then within your company.

results.title: Building Reproducible Research Pipelines in R: From Data Collection to Reporting
results.content: # Building Reproducible Research Pipelines in R: From Data Collection to Reporting. Reproducibility is a cornerstone of credible research, allowing others to verify findings by using the same data and methods. R is an excellent tool for building reproducible research workflows, thanks to its extensive libraries, accessible syntax, and robust community support. For a better idea as to why it is we are interested in being able to build reproducible research pipelines with R:. * **Transparency**: This involves documenting every step of your research, including data sources and analytical methods. * **Automation**: Minimize manual steps by automating data collection and analysis. * **Version Control**: Use tools like Git to keep track of changes in your code and documents. Data collection is the foundational step in any research project. R offers robust tools for gathering data from various sources, such as APIs, websites, and databases. This code retrieves JSON data from an API, converts it into a data frame, and saves it as a CSV file for subsequent use. library(dplyr) clean_data <- function(data) {   # Remove duplicates   data <- distinct(data)   # Fill missing values with a default value   data[is.na(data)] <- 0   return(data) } raw_data <- read.csv("data/raw_data.csv") cleaned_data <- clean_data(raw_data) write.csv(cleaned_data, "data/processed_data.csv", row.names = FALSE). This script cleans the data by removing duplicate records and handling missing values, preparing it for analysis. This includes exploratory data analysis (EDA), statistical modeling, and creating visualizations. * **Automation**: Use **knitr** to integrate analysis and reporting in one workflow. library(targets) # source("R/functions.R") # Load user-defined functions list(   tar_target(name = raw_data, command = read.csv("data/raw.csv")),   tar_target(name = cleaned_data, command = clean_data(raw_data)),   tar_target(name = model, command = lm(y ~ x, data = cleaned_data)),   tar_target( name = report, command = { rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd") "report.Rmd" # Return path to trigger dependent steps }, format = "file" ) ). ## Wrapping Up. Building reproducible research pipelines in R is essential for ensuring transparency, efficiency, and trust in scientific findings. This approach integrates data collection, analysis, and reporting into a single, seamless workflow. R provides a powerful suite of tools—including the **tidyverse**, **ggplot2**, **knitr**, and **rmarkdown**—that empower researchers to create transparent and reproducible workflows. Automating tasks like data cleaning, analysis, and visualization with well-documented scripts speeds up research and ensures consistency.
